title: Caring for the environment: food webs, soil and water
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers NIOS Class 3 'Conservation of Environment' (useful animals and their care; plant parts and uses; food chain and food web; conserving the environment and water). No textbook needed.
summary: Your child finds out how much we take from animals and plants, and asks what we give back. They learn to care for animals safely, find every part of a plant in the kitchen, watch leaf pieces float up as they make oxygen, and build food chains and a string food web. They learn that decomposers and scavengers close every loop, that taking away one creature can change everything (the starfish, the wolves and India's vultures), and that poison travels up a food chain. They finish by testing how roots hold soil and how much water a running tap wastes.
builds_on: Class 2 rung: every living thing needs a habitat with food, water and shelter; litter rots or doesn't; reduce, reuse, recycle; the Chipko women. This rung adds food chains and webs, decomposers, balance and keystone species, pollution, and conserving soil, forests and water. In Class 5: soil erosion and soil pollution in depth, forests, the greenhouse effect, a green school, and the Earth as one shared home.
goals: By the end your child can name what animals and plants give us, and say how to care for animals kindly and safely.
By the end your child can name the parts of a plant we eat and use, and show that leaves give out oxygen in sunlight.
By the end your child can build a food chain and a food web, using the words producer, consumer, herbivore, carnivore, omnivore and decomposer.
By the end your child can explain what happens when one link in a food web is removed, using a real example.
By the end your child can describe how pollution harms air, water and soil, and show how roots protect soil.
By the end your child can suggest ways to conserve forests, soil and water, and question the word 'useful'.

an animal that lives with people, like a cow, dog, hen or goat
a living thing that makes its own food from sunlight: a plant
a living thing that gets its food by eating others
an animal that eats only plants
an animal that eats other animals
an animal that eats both plants and animals

days.title: Gifts, and what we give back
days.goal: Recall Class 2, meet the story, and count what animals and plants give us.

steps.title: What do we remember?
steps.do: Recall the Class 2 rung in one quick round. Ask: 'What three things does every habitat give an animal?' (Food, water, shelter.) 'What happened to the banana peel and the plastic in the soil?' (The peel rotted; the plastic stayed.) 'Who were the Chipko women?' (Village women in the Himalayas who stopped their forest being cut.) Say: 'This time we find out who eats whom, and what happens when one kind of living thing disappears.'

steps.title: Story: The Cleaners of the Sky
steps.do: Read the story aloud. Don't explain it. Ask: 'Why did the dogs and the sickness come?' and 'Was the old vulture useful?' Write down your child's answers; you'll come back to them on Day 5.

steps.title: Breakfast gift sort
steps.do: Do Activity a1. Look at today's breakfast and the kitchen shelf, and sort everything into three columns on paper: from animals (milk, curd, ghee, eggs, honey, wool in a shawl, leather in a belt), from plants (rice, idli or dosa batter, ragi, dal, coconut, banana, coffee or tea, sugar, cotton, wood, turmeric), and from neither (salt, water, steel). Count each column. Ask: 'Which column is longest?'

steps.title: Set up: the rotting bottle
steps.do: Set up Experiment e1: in a clear plastic bottle or jar, put a layer of damp soil, then a piece of bread, a slice of fruit or vegetable peel, a dry leaf and a small piece of plastic, pressed against the side so you can see them. Close the lid. Ask your child to predict which will change first. Keep it in a shady place. Also sow a spoonful of methi seeds thickly in a tray of soil, and water it every day: you need its roots for the soil test on Day 7.

steps.title: Is a spider useful?
steps.do: Ask: 'Which animals are useful to us?' Your child will name cows, hens, bees. Then ask: 'Is a spider useful? A vulture? A mosquito? A snake?' Then the deeper question: 'Useful to whom? Would a frog say a mosquito is useful?' Leave it open.

need: the breakfast table and kitchen shelf
a clear bottle or jar with a lid, soil, bread, peel, a dry leaf, a piece of plastic
a spoonful of methi seeds and a small tray of soil

days.title: Living with animals
days.goal: Learn how to care for animals kindly and safely, and argue about cages.

steps.title: Domestic and wild
steps.do: Ask your child to sort the animals they know into domestic (living with people: cow, buffalo, goat, dog, cat, hen, camel, horse) and wild (living on their own: tiger, sparrow, monkey, snake, frog, elephant). Ask: 'What does a cow need from the family who keeps her?' (Food, clean water, shade, a clean place to stand, care when she is ill, and not being overworked.) Then the safety rules, said clearly: never tease or chase a dog; don't go near a mother dog with puppies or an animal that is eating; if any animal scratches or bites you, tell a grown-up straight away, wash the wound with soap and running water for a long time (about 15 minutes) and go to a doctor the same day, because a bite can spread rabies, which can be prevented with injections.

steps.title: Interview an animal carer
steps.do: Phone or visit someone who looks after animals: a milkman or dairy farmer, a person who feeds street dogs, a pet owner, or someone at an animal shelter. Your child asks three questions they prepare: 'What does your animal need every day? What makes it ill? What has it taught you?' Write the answers down.

steps.title: Should birds live in cages?
steps.do: Have a short debate. Your child argues one side for 2 minutes, then switches and argues the other. For cages: the bird is safe from cats and gets food. Against: a bird's habitat is the whole sky; it can't fly, find a mate or choose its food. Then tell them that in India it is against the law to keep most wild Indian birds, such as parakeets, as pets. Ask: 'What would the parakeet say?'

steps.title: Peek at the rotting bottle
steps.do: Look at Experiment e1. Has anything changed? Is there any fuzz on the bread yet? Draw what you see.

steps.title: What do we give back?
steps.do: Ask: 'Yesterday we counted what animals and plants give us. What do we give back to them?' Write down every answer your child thinks of. Some families say thank you before a meal; some leave water for birds in summer. Ask: 'Is that enough?'

days.title: Plants: the parts we use, and the oxygen they make
days.goal: Find every part of a plant in the kitchen and see leaf pieces give out oxygen.

steps.title: Kitchen plant-part hunt
steps.do: Hunt in the kitchen and sort what you find by which part of the plant it is: root (carrot, radish, beetroot, sweet potato, tapioca), stem (potato, ginger, sugarcane), leaf (spinach, curry leaves, drumstick leaves, coriander, cabbage, tea), flower (cauliflower, banana flower), fruit (mango, tomato, brinjal, lady's finger, drumstick, coconut), seed (rice, ragi, toor dal, mustard, groundnut). An onion is a short stem with thick leaf bases wrapped around it. Ask: 'Why is a potato a stem and not a root?' (It has eyes, which are buds, and it grows from the stem underground.) Ask: 'What else do plants give us that we don't eat?' (Wood, cotton, rubber, paper, medicine, shade, oxygen.)

steps.title: Bubbles from a leaf
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Cut small discs from a spinach leaf with a straw. Use a syringe to pull the air out of them, so they sink in baking soda water. Put one glass in bright sunlight and one in a dark cupboard. Ask: 'What do you think will happen to the discs in each glass?' Over 10 to 20 minutes, the discs in the sun float up one by one. Ask: 'What made them float?' (Bubbles of oxygen, made by the leaf as it makes food from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide.) Say: 'Plants are called producers because they make their own food. Almost every other living thing depends on them, and the oxygen you breathe was made by plants and by tiny algae in the sea.'

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1: animals, plants and what they give. Read each question aloud if needed.

need: vegetables, fruits, seeds and spices from the kitchen
a spinach leaf, a straw, a plastic syringe without a needle, two glasses of water, baking soda, washing-up liquid

days.title: Who eats whom?
days.goal: Build food chains and a food web, and see what happens when one strand is cut.

steps.title: Plant-eaters, meat-eaters, both
steps.do: Explain: 'A food chain shows who eats whom. It always starts with a plant, the producer. Animals are consumers.' Sort animals: herbivores (cow, deer, goat, grasshopper, elephant), carnivores (tiger, frog, spider, owl, snake), omnivores (crow, bear, human, hen, monkey). Write one chain: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle. Ask: 'Why does every chain start with a plant?' (Only plants can make food from sunlight.)

steps.title: A string food web
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Write 10 living things from a forest or a garden on cards (grass, neem tree, grasshopper, caterpillar, sparrow, frog, snake, mongoose, owl, mushroom), and lay them in a circle. Join every 'is eaten by' pair with a piece of string or wool. Add the mushroom joined to everything, because decomposers eat all dead things. Then pull one string tight by lifting the frog card: everything joined to it moves. Ask: 'If all the frogs disappeared, who would be hungry? Who would have more to eat?'

steps.title: Food Web Families
steps.do: Play the card game g1. Each player builds the longest correct food chain they can. Ask for the reason for every arrow.

steps.title: What if the frogs vanish?
steps.do: Ask: 'If all the frogs were caught and sold, what would happen to the insects? To the snakes? To the farmers' crops?' (More insects, so more crop damage; fewer snakes, or snakes eating other things.) Then: 'Is a human part of a food web? Where?'

steps.title: Rotting bottle
steps.do: Look at Experiment e1. Is there mould on the bread or peel now? Explain: 'Mould is a fungus, a decomposer. It is eating the bread.'

days.title: When one kind of creature is taken away
days.goal: Find out what happens when one creature is taken away: the starfish and the vultures.

steps.title: Paine's starfish
steps.do: Talk about voice v1, Robert Paine. Draw the rocky shore: starfish eat mussels; mussels crowd everything else out. Ask before telling: 'What do you think happened when Paine kept pulling the starfish off?' Then tell the result and ask the voice question.

steps.title: Where did the vultures go?
steps.do: Talk about voice v2, the vulture crash, and go back to the story. Ask: 'In the story, how did a medicine for cows reach the vultures?' (The cows were given diclofenac; when they died, vultures ate the meat and the medicine damaged their kidneys.) Ask: 'Why did dogs and rabies increase?' (Without vultures, dead animals lay rotting, and more stray dogs fed on them and multiplied.) Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: Deer and tigers: a running game
steps.do: Play outside or in a big room. Most players are deer, one is a tiger (a parent can be the tiger with a younger child as deer, then swap). Grass is a few cushions or chalk circles; deer must touch grass to survive a round, the tiger must catch a deer. Caught deer become tigers next round; tigers that catch nothing become grass. Count deer and tigers each round on paper. After six rounds, look at the numbers: they rise and fall, but neither disappears. Ask: 'What would happen with no tigers at all?' (Deer would multiply, eat all the grass, then starve.)

steps.title: Decomposers at work
steps.do: Look closely at Experiment e1 with a magnifying glass if you have one. Ask: 'Which things are rotting? Which haven't changed? Who is doing the rotting?' (Bacteria and fungi, tiny decomposers.) Say: 'Decomposers, and scavengers like vultures, close the loop. They turn dead things back into soil for the plants.'

need: chalk or cushions for the game

days.title: Poison that travels
days.goal: See how poison climbs a food chain, and spot pollution in air, water and soil.

steps.title: The woman who listened to the birds
steps.do: Talk about voice v3, Rachel Carson. Explain: 'DDT was sprayed to kill insects. Carson showed that it didn't stay where it was sprayed.' Ask the voice question.

steps.title: The poison bead game
steps.do: Do Activity a3. Put 1 bead (poison) on each of 20 small paper 'plankton'. Five 'fish' each eat 4 plankton, and collect their beads. Then one 'heron' eats all 5 fish. Count the heron's beads. (20.) Ask: 'Each plankton had only one bead. Why does the heron have so many?' (Poison builds up as it goes up the chain, because each eater eats many of the ones below.) Say: 'This is why the vultures were hurt by a medicine given to cows, and why Carson's birds laid eggs with thin shells.'

steps.title: Pollution spotting walk
steps.do: Walk for 10 minutes and look for pollution of air (smoke from vehicles, burning rubbish, dust), water (dirty drains, foam or rubbish in a stream or pond) and soil (plastic and rubbish on the ground, spilled oil). Your child marks each on a three-column chart. Ask: 'Where does the smoke go? Where does the drain go?' (Smoke spreads into the air we all breathe. Most drains lead to a river, a lake or the sea.)

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2: webs, balance and pollution in new places.

need: 20 small beads, buttons or tamarind seeds

days.title: Saving soil, forests and water
days.goal: Test how roots hold soil, argue about the wolves, and measure wasted water.

steps.title: Bare soil or covered soil?
steps.do: Do Experiment e3. Fill two trays or cut milk cartons with the same soil. Tilt each one on a few books wrapped in a plastic bag, with a cut opening at the low end over a cup. One tray is bare soil. The other is covered with a thick layer of leaves, or has methi seeds sown in it on Day 1, which will have roots by now. Pour a mug of water slowly on each, from the same height, like rain. Compare the water in the cups. Ask: 'Which cup is muddy? Where did that mud come from?' (The bare soil washed away: erosion. Roots and leaves hold soil and slow the rain.)

steps.title: Act it out: roots holding soil
steps.do: Two or three family members stand close and link arms tightly, like roots holding soil. Your child is the rain and tries gently to pull one person away. Then the 'roots' let go of each other and stand apart, and the rain pulls one away easily. Ask: 'What happens to soil when the trees are cut?'

steps.title: Did the wolves change the rivers?
steps.do: Talk about voice v4, the wolves of Yellowstone. Present both sides fairly and ask the voice question. Tell your child: 'Scientists are still arguing about this. You can decide what evidence would settle it.'

steps.title: How much water does brushing take?
steps.do: Do Experiment e4. Put a bucket under the bathroom tap. While your child brushes their teeth (about two minutes), let the tap run into the bucket as fast as it usually runs while brushing. Count how many mugs of water are in the bucket. Then your child brushes using just one mug of water. Ask: 'How many mugs did we save?' Multiply that by the number of people in the family, then by 2 brushings a day, then by 365 days. Use the saved water for the plants or for mopping.

need: two trays or milk cartons, soil from a pot, a few books in a plastic bag, two cups
a thick layer of fallen leaves, or methi seeds sown on Day 1

days.title: Finish the mural and teach it back
days.goal: Finish the food web mural, try the challenge worksheet, and teach it back.

steps.title: Our food web mural
steps.do: Finish the project: your child adds the last arrows to the food web mural of your own neighbourhood, including decomposers and humans, and colours producers green, herbivores yellow, carnivores red, omnivores orange and decomposers brown. Ask: 'Which creature has the most arrows? What would happen if it disappeared?'

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3. The last questions have no single right answer: ask for reasons and evidence.

steps.title: Check questions
steps.do: Ask the check questions aloud. Let your child use the mural, the rotting bottle and the erosion trays to explain.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child teaches the family: what a food chain is, what decomposers do, what happened to India's vultures, and one way our family will conserve soil, forests or water. Finish by asking again: 'Is a vulture useful?' and compare with the answer on Day 1.

experiments.title: The rotting bottle
experiments.question: What breaks down dead things, and what can't it break down?
need: a slice of fruit or vegetable peel
a lid, or a plastic bag and a rubber band
steps: Put a layer of damp soil in the jar.
Press the bread, peel, leaf and plastic against the side so they show.
Close the lid tightly, or cover the top with a plastic bag and a rubber band.
Keep it in a shady spot.
Look every two days for 10 days and draw what you see.
Do not open it. At the end, throw it away still closed.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which will change first? Which won't change at all?'
experiments.observe: Fuzzy mould grows on the bread and peel within a few days. The peel goes soft and dark. The dry leaf changes very little, because leaves take weeks to rot. The plastic stays exactly the same.
experiments.why: Mould is a fungus; with bacteria, it feeds on dead plant and animal matter and breaks it into simple materials that become soil. These decomposers, along with scavengers like vultures and crows, close the loop of every food web, returning what living things borrowed. They cannot digest plastic.
experiments.safety: Keep the jar closed, and don't sniff or touch the mould. Throw it away closed and wash hands.

experiments.title: Bubbles from a leaf
experiments.question: Do leaves give out oxygen in sunlight?
need: a plastic syringe without a needle (about 10 rupees at a chemist)
steps: Stir a pinch of baking soda and one drop of washing-up liquid into each glass of water. The baking soda gives the leaf carbon dioxide.
Press the straw through the leaf to cut 20 small discs.
Take the plunger out, drop 10 discs into the syringe and put the plunger back. Suck up some baking soda water, then push out the air.
Close the tip with a finger and pull the plunger hard for a few seconds. This pulls the air out of the discs. Repeat until they sink.
Push the discs and water into one glass and put it in bright sun. Do the same with the other 10 discs and put that glass in a dark cupboard.
Count the floating discs in each glass every 5 minutes for 20 minutes.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will the sunken discs stay at the bottom? Will the dark glass be different?'
experiments.observe: In the sun, tiny bubbles form on the discs and they float up one by one, most within 20 minutes. In the dark, the discs stay at the bottom.
experiments.why: In light, a leaf uses water and carbon dioxide to make sugar (its food) and gives out oxygen. This is photosynthesis. The oxygen fills the spaces inside the disc, so it floats. In the dark the leaf cannot make food, so no oxygen is made. Almost every food chain on Earth begins with photosynthesis.

experiments.title: Bare soil or covered soil?
experiments.question: Do plants and leaves protect soil from rain?
need: two trays or cut milk cartons
the same soil for both, from a pot or a bag of potting soil
a thick layer of fallen leaves, or methi seeds sown in the soil a week before
a few books in a plastic bag
steps: Fill both trays with soil and cut a small opening at one end.
Cover one with leaves or methi seedlings. Leave the other bare.
Tilt both on the books with the opening over a cup.
Pour one mug of water slowly from the same height on each.
Compare the water collected in the cups.
experiments.observe: The bare tray's water is brown and full of soil; the covered tray's water is much clearer and there is less of it.
experiments.why: Raindrops hit bare soil hard and loosen it, and running water carries it away: erosion. Roots bind soil and leaves break the fall of the rain, so more water soaks in and less soil is lost. Good topsoil takes hundreds of years to form and can wash away in one season.
experiments.safety: Do it on a balcony or in the bathroom, and wash hands after.

experiments.title: How much water does brushing take?
experiments.question: How much water do we save by closing the tap while brushing?
steps: Put the bucket under the bathroom tap.
While your child brushes, let the tap run into the bucket.
Count the mugs of water in the bucket.
Brush again using only one mug of water.
Work out how much the family would save in a year.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'How many mugs will run out while you brush?'
experiments.observe: A running tap fills many mugs in two minutes. One mug is enough to brush.
experiments.why: A tap can run several litres a minute. Small habits, repeated by many people every day, add up to huge amounts of water that came from rivers and groundwater shared with every living thing.

activities.title: Breakfast gift sort
need: the breakfast table and kitchen shelf
steps: Make three columns: from animals, from plants, from neither.
Sort every food and thing you can see.
Count each column.
Add one thing we could give back to animals or plants.
activities.outcome: A list showing how much of our life comes from other living things.

activities.title: A string food web
steps: Write one living thing on each card.
Lay the cards in a circle.
Tape string from each eaten thing to its eater.
Join a mushroom card to everything as the decomposer.
Lift one card and see what moves.
activities.outcome: A web that shows how every living thing is tied to many others.

activities.title: The poison bead game
steps: Put one bead on each paper 'plankton'.
Five 'fish' each take four plankton and their beads.
One 'heron' takes all five fish's beads.
Count the beads at each level and draw a pyramid.
activities.outcome: A clear picture of how poison builds up along a food chain.

voices.idea: Starting in 1963, on the rocky shore of Makah Bay in Washington State, Paine kept pulling purple starfish off one stretch of rock and throwing them back into the sea, while leaving a nearby stretch alone. Without the starfish to eat them, mussels spread and crowded out almost everything else: the number of kinds of creatures on his stretch fell from 15 to 8 within a few years. He called creatures like this starfish 'keystone species', after the stone at the top of an arch that holds the rest in place.
voices.then: Many ecologists at the time thought that the plants at the bottom of a food chain mattered most, and that predators at the top were not very important.
voices.now: Accepted. Keystone species have been found in many habitats, such as sea otters in kelp forests. Paine's way of testing, removing one creature and watching, is used all over the world.
voices.ask: Paine kept a stretch of shore where he didn't remove the starfish. Why was that important for his test?

voices.who: Vibhu Prakash and the scientists who solved India's vulture crash (1990s–2000s)
voices.idea: In the 1990s Vibhu Prakash of the Bombay Natural History Society noticed that vultures in Keoladeo National Park, Bharatpur, were dying. Surveys showed that India's white-rumped vultures, once among the commonest big birds in the world, fell by more than 95% in about 15 years. In 2004 a team led by Lindsay Oaks, working in Pakistan, found the cause: diclofenac, a painkiller given to sick cattle. Vultures that ate the carcasses of treated cattle died of kidney failure.
voices.then: At first some people blamed a disease. Finding the real cause took years of careful testing of dead birds.
voices.now: Accepted. India banned diclofenac for animals in 2006. Breeding centres such as the one at Pinjore in Haryana are raising vultures to release, but numbers are still a tiny part of what they were, and other harmful animal painkillers are still being found.
voices.ask: The medicine was meant to help cows. How could the people who made it have found out it might harm vultures? Whose job should it be to check?

voices.who: Rachel Carson (1907–1964), marine biologist and writer, USA
voices.idea: In her book 'Silent Spring' (1962) Carson gathered evidence that pesticides such as DDT, sprayed on farms and towns to kill insects, did not stay where they were sprayed. They washed into rivers and built up in the bodies of fish and birds. Birds of prey laid eggs with shells so thin they broke. She imagined a spring with no birdsong.
voices.then: Chemical companies spent large sums attacking her and called her hysterical and unscientific. She was ill with cancer while she defended her work in front of the US Congress.
voices.now: Accepted. The USA banned DDT for farm use in 1972, and birds like the bald eagle recovered. DDT is still allowed in a few countries, including India, only to kill malaria-carrying mosquitoes, and experts still debate when that is worth it.
voices.ask: The companies who made DDT said it was safe. Carson said it wasn't. If you were a judge, what evidence would you ask each side to show?

voices.who: The wolves of Yellowstone: William Ripple and Robert Beschta, and their critics (USA, 1995 onwards)
voices.idea: Wolves were brought back to Yellowstone National Park in 1995–96, about 70 years after they had been killed off there. Ripple and Beschta argued that the wolves made the elk move around more and graze less by the rivers, so willows and aspen trees grew back, beavers returned, and even the riverbanks changed shape. This chain of effects is called a trophic cascade.
voices.then: The story became hugely popular, with videos saying 'wolves changed rivers'.
voices.now: Debated. Other scientists, such as Arthur Middleton and Matthew Kauffman, found that elk were not as scared of wolves as claimed, and that hunting by people, bears and cougars, dry years, and the loss of beavers mattered too. Most agree the wolves had some effect; how big it was is still argued.
voices.ask: Why do people love a story where one hero animal fixes everything? What evidence would you need to be sure it was the wolves?

project.title: Our neighbourhood food web mural
steps: On a big sheet, draw every living thing you have seen near your home this week: plants, insects, birds, animals, fungi, people.
Draw an arrow from each living thing to the one that eats it.
Add decomposers (mould, mushrooms, earthworms) and join them to everything that dies.
Colour producers green, herbivores yellow, carnivores red, omnivores orange and decomposers brown.
Find the creature with the most arrows and write what would happen if it disappeared.
Put yourself somewhere in the web and explain where.
project.outcome: A wall mural of your own neighbourhood's food web.

game.title: Food Web Families
rules: Shuffle the cards and deal 5 to each player. Put the rest face down.
On your turn, take one card from the pile.
Lay down a food chain of at least 3 cards in the right order (producer first) and say why each one eats the next.
A chain scores 1 point per card. Adding a decomposer at the end scores 2 extra points.
If you can't make a chain, keep collecting. When the pile is empty, the most points wins.
Bonus round: lay all the chains together and find where they join into a web.

story.title: The Cleaners of the Sky
text: I am an old vulture now, and I live in a very large cage at Pinjore, at the foot of the hills in Haryana. The cage is as tall as a tree and as long as a cricket ground, with branches to sit on and a pool to drink from. The people who look after me are kind. They feed me clean meat and weigh my eggs and write numbers in a book. But I remember the sky.

When I was young, the sky over Rajasthan was full of us. You could look up on any hot afternoon and see a hundred of us turning on the warm air, round and round, so high that we were only dots, with our wings spread wide and never once flapping. We are white-rumped vultures. People thought we were ugly, with our bare grey heads and our long necks. They thought we were dirty, because of what we eat. But we were the cleaners of the sky.

Here is what we did. When a cow or a buffalo or a camel died, out in the fields or by the road, the people dragged it to the edge of the village. A family there, the leather workers, took the skin to make shoes and drums. Then they stepped back and looked up. And we came. We came down out of the sky like a slow brown rain, dozens of us, and in less than an hour there was nothing left but clean white bones in the sun. The leather workers and the vultures. We were partners, though nobody ever called it that.

A boy called Kishan, whose father was one of those leather workers, used to sit on the wall and watch us. He was not afraid. He gave us names. He called me Badi Amma, because I was the biggest. 'You eat so fast,' he said to me once, 'that the flies don't even get a chance.' I think that was the nicest thing anyone ever said to a vulture.
Then something began to go wrong, and none of us understood it.

One of my sisters sat down on a branch one morning, with her head hanging low, and did not fly. In a few days she was dead. Then another. Then a whole tree of us near the village, where we had nested for as long as anyone remembered, went silent. Each year there were fewer dots in the sky. The ones who lived laid eggs, but often no chicks hatched. I flew further and further looking for my kind, and found fewer and fewer.
Kishan noticed. He was older now, nearly twelve. 'Bapu,' I heard him say, 'where have the gidh gone?'

Without us, the dead animals lay at the edge of the village for days, and then weeks. The smell was terrible. The flies came in clouds. And the dogs came. Stray dogs had always been around, but now there was so much food for them that they had more and more puppies. Soon there were packs of them, thin and quick and quarrelsome, at the dump and in the lanes. Kishan's little sister, Pinky, was bitten on the leg by one of them while she was carrying water. She had to have a whole set of injections in the hospital in town, against rabies, and she cried every time. She was all right in the end. But Kishan sat on the wall that evening for a long time, looking at the empty sky.

It took the scientists years to find out what was killing us. They counted our nests in Bharatpur and found us vanishing. They cut open the bodies of dead vultures and found our kidneys had failed. At last they found the answer, and it was the strangest thing. It was a medicine. Farmers had begun giving their sick cows a painkiller called diclofenac, to help them stand and work when they were old or hurt. It was a kind thing to do for a cow. But when a cow died with the medicine still inside her, and we ate her, the medicine stayed inside us too. For a cow it was a little help. For a vulture, it was poison. A tiny bit, in every meal, from every carcass, and our bodies could not get rid of it.
Nobody had meant to hurt us. That was the hardest part to understand. Nobody had even thought about us at all.

I was one of the last ones they caught, out near Bikaner, a few of us still alive. They brought us here to Pinjore, to keep us safe and to try to raise chicks who might, one day, fly free over a cleaner land. The medicine is banned for animals now. Things are slowly changing.

Last spring, after many years, an egg of mine hatched. The chick is ugly, as all vulture chicks are, grey and fluffy and cross. I feed her and keep her warm. Sometimes, on a hot afternoon, I spread my wings in the cage, and she watches me, puzzled. I am showing her the shape of the sky.

I do not know if she will ever see it full of us again. But I know what we were for. We were not beautiful and we were not loved. We were the end of every story, the ones who came last and made everything clean, so that it could all begin again.
story.epiphany: The old vulture, a creature people call ugly and dirty, shows the child a food web from its least-loved strand. The turn comes when the vultures vanish: carcasses rot, dogs multiply, and Kishan's sister is bitten. The hidden ideas: scavengers and decomposers close the loop of every food web; removing one creature changes everything else; and a poison (a medicine for cows) can travel up a food chain and harm animals no one was thinking about. The quiet lenses: the leather workers and the vultures, both doing the 'dirty' work that kept the village clean, and both rarely thanked; and the question of who is 'useful'.
ask: What job did the vultures do? Who else did that job with them?
Why did the dogs and the sickness come when the vultures went?
How did a medicine meant to help cows harm the vultures?
'Nobody had even thought about us at all.' What does the vulture mean?
Was Badi Amma useful? Was she beautiful? Does it matter?

ideas.idea: Everything eats and is eaten, and everything is joined.
ideas.more: Food chains always start with plants, the producers, and end with decomposers who turn the dead back into soil. Joined together, they make a food web. In the string web, lifting one card moved many others.

ideas.idea: In nature, dead things are not wasted.
ideas.more: Scavengers and decomposers close the loop: the rotting bottle shows mould and bacteria eating what has died. When they disappear, like India's vultures, the loop breaks and problems spread.

ideas.idea: One small creature can hold a whole habitat together.
ideas.more: Paine's starfish, India's vultures and perhaps Yellowstone's wolves show that taking away one kind of creature can change many others, sometimes in ways no one predicted.

ideas.idea: Poison doesn't stay where you put it.
ideas.more: It travels through soil, water and food chains, and builds up in the animals at the top. The bead game makes this visible.

unknowns: How many kinds of creatures can a food web lose before it falls apart? Ecologists still argue about this, and the answer seems to be different in every habitat.

Will India's vultures come back? Breeding centres have raised hundreds of birds, but nobody knows yet whether released vultures can survive and multiply, because other harmful painkillers are still being given to cattle.
How much did the wolves really change Yellowstone? Scientists are still collecting evidence and disagree.
big: Which animal is the most useful? Useful to whom?
Is a human part of the food web, or outside it?
If a vulture, a tiger and a cow could vote on how we farm, what would each one say?
Is it ever right to remove one kind of animal from a place to save another?
What do we give back to the plants and animals that give us everything?

challenge.hint: Vultures clean up dead animals quickly, before germs spread and before stray dogs and rats multiply. When India lost almost all its vultures, rotting carcasses and dogs increased, and so did rabies. Ask: why do we find some animals beautiful and others ugly? Does nature care?

challenge.q: 'Survival of the fittest means the strongest animal always wins.'
challenge.hint: Nature runs on cooperation as well as competition. Bees and flowers help each other; fungi and tree roots swap food; the vultures and the leather workers did one job together. 'Fittest' in science means best suited to a place, not strongest. Ask: can you find three living things near you that help each other?

challenge.q: 'If we leave nature alone, it stays in perfect balance and never changes.'
challenge.hint: Nature is always changing: numbers of deer and tigers go up and down (the running game), forests grow back after fires, rivers move. 'Balance' means it keeps adjusting, not that it stays still. But humans can push changes much faster than nature can adjust. Ask: what is the difference between change and damage?

perspectives.view: For generations, leather workers took the skins of dead cattle, worked alongside the vultures, and kept villages clean, yet they were often treated badly for doing it. Ask: why are the people who do the most necessary 'dirty' work often the least respected?

By tradition, Parsis lay their dead in Towers of Silence, where vultures returned the bodies to nature. When the vultures disappeared, the community had to search for new ways to keep their tradition. Ask: how does losing one bird change people's lives in ways you'd never guess?

Insects can destroy a whole crop and a family's income. Spraying helps this year, but can kill the frogs, birds and spiders that eat pests for free. Ask: what would help the farmer and the frogs at the same time?

Charles Darwin spent years studying earthworms and wrote that few animals have played such an important part in the history of the world. They drag leaves underground and turn them into soil. Ask: if earthworms could talk, what would they say about the swept, bare garden?

check.q: Name three things we get from animals and three from plants.
check.a: For example, milk, wool, honey; rice, cotton, wood.

check.q: What should you do if an animal bites or scratches you?
check.a: Tell a grown-up, wash the wound with soap and running water for a long time, and see a doctor the same day.
They make their own food from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide, and give out oxygen.

check.q: Give a food chain with a herbivore and a carnivore in it.
check.a: For example, grass → deer → tiger, or grass → grasshopper → frog → snake.

check.q: What do decomposers and scavengers do?
check.a: They break down or eat dead things and return them to the soil, closing the loop.

check.q: What happened when India's vultures disappeared, and why did they disappear?
check.a: A cattle painkiller, diclofenac, poisoned them; carcasses rotted, stray dogs and rabies increased.

check.q: How do trees and grass protect soil?
check.a: Their roots hold the soil and their leaves soften the rain, so less soil washes away.
